summary: Connect an AI assistant to the catalog of motion videos and prompts and to the technique articles through a read-only MCP server, or read the same data as plain JSON.
markdown:
# Use the warehouse from an AI

An assistant can search the catalog (about 800 motion videos with the prompts that made them) and read the technique articles without opening this site. Everything is read-only and public: no sign-in, nothing to install for the remote server.

## Connect with MCP

The server speaks MCP over HTTP at one address:

```
https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/mcp
```

In Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http warehouse https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/mcp
```

Other clients that accept a server URL take the same address. A local server over stdio is also available (see below).

## What it can do

| Tool | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| `search_videos` | Find videos by words, category, tag, source or whether a remake exists. Returns short summaries and pages through the results |
| `get_video` | Get one video: the full generation prompt, author, tags, and links to the original, the remake, the poster and the how and style documents |
| `get_video_doc` | Read the how or style document of a video as markdown |
| `list_filters` | List the categories, sources and tags, with counts |
| `list_techniques` | List the technique articles, the hub and the skills list |
| `get_technique` | Read one of those pages as markdown |
| `search_techniques` | Search the articles by words and get a snippet around each hit |

Questions that work well: "Find three.js shader videos and show me the prompt of the best one", "Which technique explains a speed ramp, and what are its numbers?", "List the categories in the video catalog".

## Plain JSON

If you would rather fetch the data yourself:

| Address | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| [/items.json](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/items.json) | The catalog: one object per video with title, author, category, tags, the prompt and links to the videos and poster |
| [/techniques.json](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/techniques.json) | Every technique article, the hub and the skills list, with a markdown body |
| [/llms.txt](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/llms.txt) | A short guide for AI clients with these addresses and the page list |

A quick check from a terminal:

```bash
curl -s https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/mcp \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search_videos","arguments":{"query":"shader","limit":3}}}'
```

## Run it locally

The same tools run as a local stdio server from the `mcp` folder of the [viewer repository](https://github.com/suenot/mvw-viewer/tree/main/mcp). It needs Node 18 or newer and can read your own copy of the warehouse instead of the public data.

```bash
claude mcp add warehouse -- node /path/to/mvw-viewer/mcp/stdio.mjs
```

## Limits

- Read-only: no tool changes data.
- A request body is capped at 100 KB and a list at 50 rows.
- Video files are not returned, only links to them.

# Motion skills: where to extract the techniques

[Video creation studies]() · [Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A skill is a prompt with taste. Our [skill trial]() found that no third-party skill beat a control built with none, and that every skill collided with the owner's rules at least once. What is worth taking is a single technique together with its evidence, and this page lists where each technique can be taken from.

Licences below were checked on the dates in the trial; they can change, so check the repository before copying anything.

[Figure, animated on the site: How to extract a technique from a skill without installing it.]

| [Blender frames](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/blender-frames) | The Blender manual and Python API; a locally installed Blender skill covers bpy, actions and F-curves, cameras, materials and linked libraries |

## Rules for taking from a skill

- **Install nothing.** An installed skill can change defaults silently, and copying files brings in licence terms. Keep the repositories as reading.
- **Read as data, run no code.** Never run an installer or a script from a skill you have not reviewed.
- **Check the licence.** AGPL and "none stated" mean reading only.
- **List conflicts first.** Each skill in the trial collided with an owner rule: a moving camera, camera travel, region highlights, never-ship items.
- **Build a control.** Make the same scene without the skill and let an independent check rank them by the owner's rules.
- **A checklist that demands change needs a fact to show.** One checklist item pushed a builder to invent a meaning on a map; the change must use facts already in the fact table.

# Motion techniques Claude can use

[Video creation studies]() · Reviewed November 16, 2026

This is the practical side of the studies: each technique the tutorials describe, pulled out as its own article with a small animated demo, so an assistant (or a person) can apply it one at a time. The main source is ProdAdvice's HyperFrames tutorial ([K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g)); we add the two other tutorials the owner picked, Studio Igor's game-art experiments ([YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk)) and Andrey Zenin's 2D video plugin tutorial ([YyUP_hSovOg](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg)). The second wave of techniques comes from a fourth tutorial found in the chat history, ИИ МАСТОДОНТ's "Sonnet 5.5 and HyperFrames" ([yEpN_s9UkAE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE)), and from the prompts in this site's own Videos catalog, mainly the detailed ones by flxrnc, techhalla and 0xnicc0 (their authors' X posts are linked in each article). The third wave comes from the owner's curves project (harmonic shapes, letters and sound, accumulated clocks) and from 3D work: our Tabletop Miniature style and a small Blender test we ran. The fourth wave comes from reading the skill repositories listed on the [skills page](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/skills) (we cloned them into a temporary folder and read the files as data, running nothing): motion defaults, an importance budget, speed ramps, downbeat cuts, B-roll treatments, lower thirds, a drawing hand, diagrams, OKLCH gradients, parallax, reduced motion and the vertical safe box. We read the transcripts, the prompts and the skills; we have not rerun them.

The skills these techniques can be pulled from, with repository links, are on [Motion skills: where to extract the techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/skills).

[Figure, animated on the site: The twelve groups of techniques: how the drawing looks, how the work is organised, how picture and voice meet, how motion is engineered, how type moves, how the work is directed and reviewed, how shapes become harmonics, how 3D is used, and four groups from the skill repositories: timing and importance, cuts and overlays, drawing and diagrams, colour, depth and access.]

## The techniques

### The pencil look

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Line boil](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/line-boil) | Redraws each outline about 12 times a second while the shape stays still | ProdAdvice 08:05, Studio Igor 0:49 |
| [Drawing cadence and a stable seed](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed) | Keeps the drawing rhythm independent of the file frame rate, and makes a re-render identical | ProdAdvice 08:22 |
| [Hatching](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/hatching) | Shades with strokes instead of a flat fill | ProdAdvice 09:00 |
| [Construction lines](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/construction-lines) | Leaves faint guides under a contour made of short broken strokes | ProdAdvice 08:05, Studio Igor 0:49 |

### The workflow

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Timing plan](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/timing-plan) | Holds every entrance, exit and path as plain numbers on one timeline | ProdAdvice 01:32 |
| [Style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract) | Turns a look into measurable tokens that every scene shares | ProdAdvice 10:14, Studio Igor 2:32 |
| [Render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect) | Checks real frames at fixed times and writes down each defect | ProdAdvice 05:00, Studio Igor 20:55 |
| [Error log](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/error-log) | Turns each failure into a check for the next scene | ProdAdvice 10:14, Studio Igor 14:14 |
| [Short pieces](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/assemble-from-pieces) | Approves scenes one at a time and reviews only the seams | ProdAdvice 10:14, Zenin 6:39 |

### Picture and voice

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Layered assets](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/layered-assets) | Painted layers for forms, code for depth, light and text | Studio Igor 7:48 |
| [One sentence, one shot](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/sentence-shot) | Cuts a fraction of a second before each sentence | Zenin 2:02 |
| [Number readout](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/number-readout) | Shows a figure small, beside what it measures | Zenin 2:26 |

### Motion engineering

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Seekable frame](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame) | Draws the picture as a pure function of time, so any moment can be frozen and checked | Prompts flxrnc, techhalla, BuildFastWithAI |
| [Closed-form springs](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs) | Moves everything with exact spring formulas; the camera is slower than the shape | Prompts flxrnc, AnnaCher, 0xnicc0 |
| [Beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid) | Puts every event on a fixed grid of beats (0.5 s at 120 BPM) | Prompts flxrnc, techhalla, 0xnicc0 |
| [Seamless loop](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seamless-loop) | Makes the last frame equal the first, cursor included | Prompts flxrnc, techhalla |
| [Subframe blur](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/subframe-blur) | Blends four samples per frame for real motion blur | Prompts flxrnc, techhalla |
| [One shape, never cut](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/one-shape) | Tells a product story with one element that morphs, with no cuts | Prompts AnnaCher, 0xnicc0, flxrnc |
| [Independent clocks](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/independent-clocks) | Gives each motion its own accumulated phase, so a speed change never moves the past | The owner's curves project |

### Type and print

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Kinetic type per glyph](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/kinetic-type) | A spring per letter, started 125 ms apart | Prompt techhalla |
| [Mask reveal](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/mask-reveal) | Turns the outgoing word into a window onto the next scene | Prompt techhalla |
| [Print misregistration](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/misregistration) | Two offset colour copies of text, on impact frames only | Prompt techhalla |

### Direction and review

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Storyboard and pre-pass](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/storyboard-first) | Storyboard before code, one still per beat before the render | Prompts flxrnc, 0xnicc0, techhalla; ИИ МАСТОДОНТ 06:04 |
| [Reference by link](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/reference-by-link) | Gives a link to a clip you like and asks for your story in that style | ИИ МАСТОДОНТ 13:10 |
| [Feedback in passes](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/feedback-passes) | Pace, then sound, then music fitted to the beat | ИИ МАСТОДОНТ 08:13 |
| [Locked message and bans](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/locked-message) | Fixes the exact words and lists what must not appear | Prompt techhalla |

### Harmonic shapes

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Harmonic morph](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/harmonic-morph) | Stores an outline as a few complex harmonics; morphs by mixing coefficients; the count is a smoothness dial | The owner's curves project |
| [Harmonic type](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/harmonic-type) | Builds letters from closed contours, filled as one even-odd compound path so holes stay open | The owner's curves project |
| [Shape to sound](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/shape-to-sound) | Uses the magnitudes of a contour's harmonics as the partials of a tone | The owner's curves project |

### 3D and Blender

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Camera curves](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/camera-curves) | Keys a 3D camera's channels with monotone Hermite curves: smooth, no overshoot, flat on holds | Our Tabletop Miniature style |
| [Tilt-shift band](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/tilt-shift) | Blurs all but one band so a scene reads as a miniature; grain seeded by frame number | Our Tabletop Miniature style |
| [Blender frames](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/blender-frames) | Scripts a headless Blender animation and renders each frame from its number | Our own test, Blender 5.2.2 |

### Timing and importance

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Motion defaults](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/motion-defaults) | Gives a default length in frames to each kind of move: opacity 6, entrance 12, blur 7, exit 10 to 13 | motionmaxxing |
| [Importance budget](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/importance-budget) | Rates every beat 1 to 3 and lets at most a quarter be 3 | motionmaxxing |

### Cuts, sound and overlays

| Technique | What it does | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- |

| [Downbeat cuts](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/downbeat-cuts) | Scenes of whole bars, cuts marked by a chord change, not by a loud accent | iart-ai javascript-animation-skills |

## How to use them

1. Start from the workflow group: a [timing plan](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/timing-plan) and a [style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract) cost minutes and prevent most rework.
2. Pick one look technique for the job and test it on one short scene. Do not stack all four of the pencil techniques on a first attempt.
3. Run [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect) on every scene, and keep the [error log](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/error-log) current.
4. For narrated pieces add the picture-and-voice group.
5. For product and UI motion, or pieces that loop or go to music, add the motion-engineering group ([seekable frame](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame) first) and the direction-and-review group.
6. For character and shape work add the harmonic group; for 3D scenes, the 3D group (the Blender article is a measured test, the others come from a finished style).
7. For short-form and talking-head work add the cuts-and-overlays group, and set [motion defaults](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/motion-defaults) and an [importance budget](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/importance-budget) before animating. Always plan a [reduced-motion](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/reduced-motion-tiers) version of anything that slides, zooms or moves in depth.

## Limits

The demos are our own drawings that show how each mechanism works. They are not frames from the tutorials, and the numbers inside them (amplitudes, spacings, pixel shifts) are illustrative unless an article says a number comes from a source. The code snippets are our proposed implementations and were not run; none of the four tutorials publishes its source, and the prompts in the catalog are given without their code. Numbers in the fourth wave (frames, decibels, pixels) are the skills' own claims, not remeasured by us. A technique that works in a demo has to be tested on a real scene, with the checks in [Auditing a video](), before it enters a client video.

Studies behind this page: [HyperFrames tutorial study](), [Layered art tutorial study](), [Reference: 2D video plugin](), [Skill trial: bond Short]().

# Technique: build long work from short approved pieces

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The creator says outright that long pieces are easier to build as smaller sections ([10:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=614s)). The tutorial on a code-drawn 2D video plugin shows the same habit from another angle: it renders a pilot of about 30 s before the full video, and the author then picks one scene of the pilot to change ([6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg&t=399s)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Four scenes of 5 s, each approved on its own, slide together into one 20 s strip. The three seams get a review flag for palette, audio and pacing.]

## How it works

1. **Split the story into scenes** of a few seconds, each with one idea. The demo uses four scenes of 5 s.
2. **Build and approve each scene alone** against the [style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract), with its own [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect) pass. A defect is found in 5 s of film, not in 20.
3. **Join them** into one timeline. The scenes share the palette, the seed rules and the audio bed.
4. **Review the seams.** With four scenes there are three. Look at the last frame of one and the first of the next, and listen for a jump in level or ambience.

## Why it helps

- A correction touches one scene, so the others are not at risk.
- Scenes are reusable: an approved opening can be placed in the next film.
- A pilot gives early feedback. Render the first 8 to 10 s at draft quality and show it before the full build; after a render, send the owner a numbered sheet with one thumbnail per shot, so feedback can name a shot (see [Reference: 2D video plugin]()).

## Watch for

- **Seams.** Matching colour, grain and sound level at the cut is the work that remains. A shared contract prevents most of it; the review catches the rest.
- **Scenes that cannot stand alone.** If scene 3 needs scene 2 to make sense, approve them as a pair.
- **Per-scene seeds that reuse the same drawing.** Two scenes with one seed will boil in lockstep. See [Drawing cadence and a stable seed](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed).

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 10:14-11:41; Andrey Zenin, [YyUP_hSovOg](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg) at 6:39-7:25. The 4 x 5 s split is our illustration.

title: Technique: a beat grid
label: Beat grid
summary: Put every move, click and sound on a fixed grid of beats so a piece without a soundtrack still feels in time, and music can be added later.
markdown:
# Technique: a beat grid

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Prompts for product motion often start from a grid of time, not from a list of effects. One gives a 0.5 s beat grid and lists what happens at each beat, from "0.0 pixel mascot idles" to "12.0 toast shrinks back into the mascot" ([flxrnc](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921)). Another sets 120 BPM and says something must land on every beat for the first 16 beats, and after that on every other beat ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)). A third wants 24 beats at 120 BPM "and something happens on every beat" ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)); a fourth syncs everything to a 128 BPM grid ([BuildFastWithAI](https://x.com/BuildFastWithAI/status/2108403445304844291)).

[Figure, animated on the site: A 4 s axis at 120 BPM: a heavy tick every 0.5 s, a light tick every 125 ms. Six events sit on beats. A hit that started at 1.3 s slides to the beat at 1.5 s.]

## How it works

At 120 BPM one beat is 0.5 s and a sixteenth note is 125 ms. If every entrance, click and impact is placed on that grid, the piece has a pulse before any sound exists, and a track at the same tempo fits with no re-timing. The 125 ms step also gives a natural stagger for [letters](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/kinetic-type).

## How to build it

Put the grid in the [timing plan](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/timing-plan) and snap to it:

```js
const BPM = 120, beat = 60 / BPM;            // 0.5 s
const onGrid = (t) => Math.round(t / beat) * beat;
const plan = { mascotSquash: onGrid(1.0), loader: onGrid(1.5), check: onGrid(2.0) };
```

With real music, find the track's own grid first: start on a downbeat and place each click and chime on a measured peak ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612) asks for exactly this, with a royalty-free track near 120 BPM).

## Watch for

- **Every beat filled for ever.** The prompt that fills the first 16 beats relaxes to every other beat afterwards. Constant hits tire the eye.
- **A grid that fights the story.** Sentences have their own timing; see [one sentence, one shot](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/sentence-shot). Use the grid for UI and motion pieces, voice timing for narrated ones.
- **Rounding the tempo.** A track at 118 BPM on a 120 BPM grid drifts out in a few bars.

**Sources:** [flxrnc-251921](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921), [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547), [0xnicc0-516612](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612), BuildFastWithAI in our prompt database; the `onGrid` snippet is ours.

markdown:
# Technique: a Blender animation as frame numbers

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Blender can sit in this workflow the way Three.js does: a 3D element made by a script, with a motion that is a function of the frame number, rendered to still images and laid into the video. Nothing in this collection covered Blender, so we ran a small test ourselves. It covers only what we measured, and the limits are listed below.

[Figure, animated on the site: The four steps of the test, and the cube position at five frames. Orange line: the default Bezier interpolation. Dashed: linear. The numbers are what the script printed.]

## What we ran

Blender 5.2.2 LTS, headless, with this script (`/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b -P test.py`):

```python
import bpy
sc = bpy.context.scene
sc.frame_start, sc.frame_end = 1, 48
sc.render.engine = "BLENDER_WORKBENCH"
sc.render.resolution_x, sc.render.resolution_y = 320, 180
cube = bpy.context.object
cube.location.x = -2; cube.keyframe_insert("location", index=0, frame=1)
cube.location.x =  2; cube.keyframe_insert("location", index=0, frame=48)

act, slot = cube.animation_data.action, cube.animation_data.action_slot
fc = next(f for f in act.layers[0].strips[0].channelbag(slot).fcurves
          if f.data_path == "location" and f.array_index == 0)
print([round(fc.evaluate(f), 3) for f in (1, 12, 24, 36, 48)])
sc.frame_set(24)                      # the scene is now exactly frame 24
sc.render.filepath = "out/"; bpy.ops.render.render(animation=True)
```

## What we measured

- **The value is a function of the frame.** With the default Bezier keys, `fc.evaluate` gave -2, -1.445, -0.064, 1.351 and 2 at frames 1, 12, 24, 36, 48. After `frame_set(5)` and then `frame_set(24)` the cube was at the same x as before.
- **Default is not linear.** The Bezier join eases in and out: at frame 12 the cube is at -1.445, where a linear join gives -1.064. For a steady travel set the keys to `LINEAR`.
- **Same frame, same file.** Frame 24 rendered twice gave identical PNG files.
- **Fast enough to iterate.** 48 frames in Workbench at 320 by 180 took 0.4 seconds. This says nothing about Eevee or Cycles at full size.
- **The curves API moved.** In 5.2.2 `action.fcurves` was not there. Curves live on a channel bag: `action.layers[0].strips[0].channelbag(slot).fcurves`. Older recipes you find online break on it.

This is the same contract as a [seekable frame](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame): render frame `n` from `n` alone. Keys placed on Bezier handles can be shaped like the [camera curves](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/camera-curves); for a rig, key the camera object the same way.

## How it fits a video

Render the 3D part as a numbered PNG sequence (a transparent background is a render setting; we did not test it) and treat it as a layer: lay it over the 2D scene, mask it, and check it frame by frame as in [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect). Use Blender when the object needs modelling, materials or physically based light. Use Three.js, as in the [camera curves](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/camera-curves) article, when the whole scene is real-time and shares the page clock.

## Not tested

Encoding to a video file, a transparent background, Eevee and Cycles, GPU rendering, rigs, simulations, and a long sequence. The Blender add-on for live control was not connected in this session, so the test used the command line only.

**Sources:** our own run, as above; [Blender Python API](https://docs.blender.org/api/current/) for the names used. The installed Blender skill documents the same area.

# Technique: three B-roll treatments and per-beat timing

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A talking-head video gets motion graphics in two decisions: what kind of layer each line gets, and when each element appears against the voice.

[Figure, animated on the site: Top, a 26 second plan made of three treatments: A speaker, B overlay, C cover (A4 B5 A5 C5 A3 B2 A2 seconds, an example). Below, the timing choice for "revenue grew 30 percent": axes lead by about six frames, the value lands on the word, an answer waits.]

## Three treatments

- **A, speaker.** The video alone. For the opening line, an opinion, an emotional beat, the call to action and the closing line.
- **B, overlay.** A transparent layer over the speaker: a keyword, a number counting up, an icon, a short list. Keep it toward the edges and out of the face.
- **C, cover.** An opaque full-frame scene hides the speaker while the voice continues. For numbers, comparisons, steps, an interface, anything with three or more parts.

Rhythm rules from the skill: open and close on A; no stretch of A longer than about 8 seconds; a C stretch runs about 3 to 8 seconds, with the speaker back between covers.

## Timing per element

| Timing | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| Lead by about six frames | Context the eye can prepare: axes, cards, process structure |
| Sync to the relevant word | New key facts: amounts, percentages, prices, final chart values |
| Wait for the reveal | Punchlines, negations, withheld answers, conclusions |

For "revenue grew 30%": bring in the chart structure early, then land the final bar value on the word "30%". Synchronization means the number is readable, not that a long count-up has started. Compare [one sentence, one shot](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/sentence-shot) and [number readout](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/number-readout).

**Sources:** [iart-ai/b-roll-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/b-roll-skills), `skills/talking-head-b-roll/SKILL.md`. MIT licence. The 26 second plan is our example.

label: Cadence and seed
summary: Why the redraw rhythm must come from time, not from the frame number, and why the random numbers must be seeded so a re-render gives the same picture.
markdown:
# Technique: drawing cadence and a stable seed

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Line boil needs two decisions that look like details and decide whether the effect survives a render. First, how often a new drawing appears, independent of the video's frame rate. Second, which random numbers a given moment uses, so that the same moment always looks the same.

## Cadence is not the frame rate

ProdAdvice contrasts 24 and 12 fps with a ball example ([08:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=502s)). The part that carries over to a production file is the idea, not the setting: the drawing rate is a look, and the file rate is a delivery format.

[Figure, animated on the site: Half a second at 12 drawings a second. The drawing rhythm stays the same; only the number of frames each drawing holds changes with the file rate.]

The drawing index is `floor(time * 12)`. In a 24 fps file each drawing holds 2 frames. In a 30 fps file the holds alternate between 3 and 2 frames. Both show the same six drawings in half a second.

## A seed makes a moment repeatable

A renderer may visit the same time more than once: it seeks, it re-renders a failed chunk, you scrub back to check a defect. If the outline uses a random number at every call, the second visit draws a different contour, and the defect you saw is gone or a new one appears.

[Figure, animated on the site: The same three visits to the timeline: 0.5 s, 1.0 s, then 0.5 s again. With a random number the third circle differs from the first; with a seed that comes from the scene seed plus the drawing index it is identical.]

The fix is one line: seed the generator with the scene seed plus the drawing index, `seed = sceneSeed + floor(time * 12)`. Then 0.5 s is drawing 6 every time, and 1.0 s is drawing 12.

## Checklist

1. Compute the drawing index from time, never from a frame counter.
2. Give each scene one fixed seed and store it with the scene, so a revision does not reshuffle every line.
3. Let the camera and any text read continuous time, not the drawing index. Only the stroke follows the cadence.
4. Do not change a required delivery rate (24, 25, 30) to imitate a source video. Keep 12 drawings a second inside the file.

This is our proposed implementation. The tutorial does not publish its code; see the source limits in [HyperFrames tutorial study]().

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 08:22.

# Technique: construction lines and broken strokes

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A real sketch shows how it was made: a light box, a cross to find the centre, a looser first circle, then a darker contour that does not quite close. ProdAdvice lists "broken strokes" and "light construction lines" among the marks that give the handmade impression ([08:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=485s)). Studio Igor's whale cartoon draws blue construction strokes before the main action ([0:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=49s)).

[Figure, animated on the site: One circle in three stages: guides (a dashed box, a cross and a looser circle), then a contour of seven short strokes with gaps, then both together with the guides left faint.]

## How it works

- **Guides** go down first and in a second colour, so they read as scaffolding. A dashed bounding box, a cross through the centre and a slightly larger, looser circle are enough.
- **The contour** is split into short strokes. In the demo there are seven, each ending a little before the next begins, with the end points moved by a seeded offset.
- **Together:** when the contour lands, the guides drop to about half their strength (opacity 0.9 to 0.45 in the demo) and stay.

The order matters for motion. Guides appear first, which gives the eye something to track; the strokes then arrive over them. A guide that appears after the contour looks like an error.

## How to build it

Treat guides as their own layer with their own opacity token. The contour function takes a stroke count and a gap size, and returns a path with several sub-paths:

```js
const strokes = 7, gap = 0.16;   // radians left open at each seam
for (let s = 0; s < strokes; s++) {
  const a0 = (s / strokes) * TAU + gap / 2, a1 = ((s + 1) / strokes) * TAU - gap / 2;
  path.push(arc(cx, cy, r, a0, a1, jitter(seed + s)));
}
```

## Watch for

- **Guides that compete with a label.** Keep them out of the area reserved for text, or fade them out before the label arrives.
- **Gaps that look like a rendering bug.** If a seam is wider than a few pixels at delivery size, reduce the gap.
- **Everything at once.** Use guides on the hero object, not on every element of the frame.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 08:05-09:09, and Studio Igor, [YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk) at 0:49-2:31. Stroke count, gap and opacity figures are from our demo.

# Technique: cuts on the downbeat, without a startle

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Two rules from one generated-soundtrack skill: where the cuts go, and how loud the music may get at a cut.

[Figure, animated on the site: Top, a strip of scenes of 2, 2 and 4 bars; each cut falls on a bar start. Below, four loudness jumps into a cut against the 6 dB line: an accent on the cut, kick and bass entering together, layers a bar apart, a chord change.]

## Where the cuts go

Each scene gets a whole number of bars (the tempo may flex per scene), so every cut lands on a downbeat. This extends the [beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid): the grid is bars, and scene lengths are multiples of a bar.

## How loud a cut may be

The skill reports its own measurements on short pieces:

- A loud accent on a cut (bass and a bright chime at once) reads as a jump scare: a jump of +7 to +10 dB was flagged as startling. A chord change with +3 to +5 dB reads as a clean edit.
- Even the normal downbeat accent tipped short pieces over +6 dB, because the bar before is still decaying. The chord change is enough.
- Kick and bass entering together after a quiet intro measured +11 dB. Staggered by a bar, +3.5 dB. Bring layers in one or two per bar.

The skill's check script fails a cut that is off the beat by more than 100 ms (about three frames) or that jumps more than +6 dB against the second before. The demo draws that threshold as a line. The bar heights are the skill's quoted figures (the accent drawn at 8.5 and the chord change at 4, the middles of the quoted ranges).

**Sources:** [iart-ai/javascript-animation-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/javascript-animation-skills), `skills/soundtrack/SKILL.md`. MIT licence.

# Technique: an error log that turns into checks

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The last item on ProdAdvice's checklist is a list of errors ([10:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=614s)). Studio Igor shows it working: when a character's hand goes behind the body while aiming upward, he adds a corrective rule to the skill ([14:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=854s)). A mistake is paid for once and then guarded against.

[Figure, animated on the site: Three concrete failures and the check each produces: a label collides with the phone crop at 3.2 s (keep labels 90 px inside the safe area), hatching flips direction between frames (one angle per object, fixed seed), text flickers as the contour redraws (labels follow continuous time).]

## How it works

Each entry has two halves:

- **What went wrong,** specific enough that someone else can find it: the thing, the symptom and the time.
- **The check it becomes,** a rule a script or an assistant can apply before it shows you anything.

Good entries name numbers and times. "Label collides with phone crop at 3.2 s" is useful; "text layout issues" is not. A vague entry cannot become a check.

## Keep it short

Do not paste an ever-growing transcript into every prompt. Cap the log at the failures that still matter, merge entries that say the same thing, and move a rule that is always true into the [style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract). Version the file with the project, so a revert brings back the matching rules.

## Make it run

The best rules are tested, not just read:

```js
if (label.box.right > frame.width - 90) fail("label inside safe area", label.id, time);
```

A rule that can fail loudly in the render step needs no one to remember it.

## Watch for

- **Rules that fight each other.** When two checks disagree, decide which wins and delete the other.
- **A log nobody feeds.** Add the entry in the same sitting as the fix, while the frame number is still in front of you.
- **Rules from a different format.** A check made for a map fact may not fit a character scene. Note the scope in the entry.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, [YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk) at 14:14-17:33. The three example entries are from our [HyperFrames tutorial study]() and are illustrations.

# Technique: feedback in passes

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The tutorial's promo was not one prompt but a process: install HyperFrames, ask for key frames, tell it to keep to the brand and give your references, then refine step by step. First feedback on which scenes are too fast, then sound and music (a few options to choose from), after which the model fitted the animation to the music so it hooks harder ([ИИ МАСТОДОНТ, 08:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=493s)). Other demos in the same video: the vertical Short took feedback such as "redraw the logo, fast in places, slow in others", and the talking-head edit began dull and improved when he asked it to be creative and not follow a template ([09:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=555s), [11:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=667s)). A prompt in our database reports the same shape: "1 prompt and 2 rounds of feedback" ([daniel_haida](https://x.com/daniel_haida/status/2104139720829636937)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Three versions. v1 has only picture, with the note that scenes are too fast. v2 adds sound to every movement. v3 adds a track cut to its beat. Each pass adds one layer.]

## How it works

A model that is asked for everything at once spreads its effort thin. One concern per pass keeps each change small enough to judge. The order matters: pace first (picture), then sound that matches visible movement, then music, which depends on pace being settled. Each pass starts from the last approved version and is checked with [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect).

## How to build it

- Pass 1: "scenes 2 and 4 are too fast; hold each for at least 1.5 s". Re-check the [timing plan](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/timing-plan).
- Pass 2: "add a sound for every visible movement" (the prompt database has one: "make every sound match a movement you can see", [adrianduta96](https://x.com/adrianduta96/status/2109187815195992248)).
- Pass 3: bring your own track or generate one without words, and ask to fit the video to the song and pick the best moments ([13:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=817s)). Put the cuts on the [beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid).
- When it feels flat: ask it to be creative and not follow a template.

## Watch for

- **Mixed notes.** "Faster, add music and change the colour" is three passes; the model will do one well.
- **Music first.** Changing pace afterwards breaks the fit.
- **Music made in code.** The author says he does not know how the model makes it and prefers his own track; one prompt in our database makes the soundtrack from sine waves and noise ([daniel_haida](https://x.com/daniel_haida/status/2104139720829636937)). Treat either as a draft to listen to.

**Sources:** ИИ МАСТОДОНТ, [yEpN_s9UkAE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE) at 08:13, 09:15, 11:07 and 13:37; [daniel-haida-636937](https://x.com/daniel_haida/status/2104139720829636937) and [adrianduta96-992248](https://x.com/adrianduta96/status/2109187815195992248) in our prompt database.

title: Technique: a hand that draws on, tip on the point
label: Hand draw-on
summary: A whiteboard draw-on: one eased value draws the stroke, and the pen sits on the point at that same value; between strokes it lifts and moves unseen.
markdown:
# Technique: a hand that draws on, tip on the point

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The VideoScribe look is a stroke that draws itself and a pen that never leaves the newest point. The trick is that both come from one number.

[Figure, animated on the site: Two strokes, each drawn as 30 line pieces that fade in one after another. The pen sits on the newest point, lifts at the end of the first stroke and travels unseen to the start of the second.]

## The mechanic

Give each path `pathLength="1"`, so a single value from 0 to 1 draws any path whatever its real length. Use a linear or very gentle ease: an ease-in-out on a long stroke makes the marker lurch. At progress `k`, sample the path at `k` and put the pen's nib there. Offset the pen art so its tip, not its corner, lands on the point. Between separate strokes lift the pen (fade out, jump, fade in) so it does not slide across blank board. Draw one thing at a time, in narration order.

## A sketch

The skill uses `stroke-dashoffset`; our demo, which animates only transform and opacity, draws 30 short pieces instead.

```js
path.setAttribute("pathLength", 1);
path.style.strokeDasharray = 1;
path.style.strokeDashoffset = 1 - k;          // k from 0 to 1
const p = path.getPointAtLength(k * path.getTotalLength());
pen.setAttribute("transform", `translate(${p.x - NIB.x} ${p.y - NIB.y})`);
```

The nib stays glued because both the stroke and the pen read the same `k`. This is the [seekable frame](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame) contract again: given `k`, the picture is known.

**Sources:** [iart-ai/explainer-video-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/explainer-video-skills), `skills/whiteboard-animation/SKILL.md`. MIT licence.

title: Technique: shapes as harmonics, and morphing between them
label: Harmonic morph
summary: Store a closed outline as a few complex harmonics, then morph between two outlines by mixing coefficients. The same list is also a smoothness dial.
markdown:
# Technique: shapes as harmonics, and morphing between them

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

This technique comes from the owner's own project, a set of small browser games where every creature, asteroid and letter is a closed outline stored as Fourier coefficients (the project is private; the maths is standard). The idea fits video as well: an outline is a list of complex numbers, and a list of numbers can be mixed.

[Figure, animated on the site: Left, a star becomes a house: the 12 largest harmonics of each outline are mixed from alpha 0 to 1, drawn as 14 in-between frames (dashed: the two full outlines). Right, the same star rebuilt from 2, 6 and 24 harmonics.]

## How it works

Walk once around a closed outline at constant speed and write each point as a complex number `x + iy`. A discrete Fourier transform turns the points into coefficients `c_k`, one per signed frequency `k`. The outline comes back as `point(t) = sum of c_k * exp(i * 2 * pi * k * t)` for `t` from 0 to 1. The `k = 0` term is the centre; `k = 1` alone is a circle; each further pair adds finer detail.

Two things follow:

- **Smoothness is a budget.** Keep the centre and the few terms with the largest magnitude, and the outline loses its fine corners but keeps its character. This is a low-pass filter on a shape. It is also a size limit: 12 numbers instead of 96 points.
- **A morph is a mix.** If two shapes use the same frequencies, `mix(a, b, alpha)` is `a + (b - a) * alpha` on the real and imaginary part of each coefficient. A frequency missing on one side counts as zero. Every in-between frame is a valid, smooth outline, and `alpha` can be eased, sprung or keyed like any other number.

## How to build it

Do the DFT once, at authoring time, and keep the coefficients:

```js
const N = 96;                                   // same sample count for every shape
const ca = selectLargest(dft(resample(star,  N)), 12);
const cb = selectLargest(dft(resample(house, N)), 12);

const pose = (t) => contour(mix(ca, cb, easeInOut(t)), 120);   // a pure function of t
ctx.fill(new Path2D(toPath(pose(t))));
```

`resample` walks the polygon and returns `N` points spaced evenly by arc length. `selectLargest` keeps the centre plus the `budget` terms of largest magnitude. `contour` evaluates the sum at `m` values of `t`.

## Watch for

- **Same start, same direction.** Both outlines must run the same way round and start at the corresponding point. The project's own notes warn that automatic alignment by closest point does not guarantee the intended match: look at the middle frames.
- **One fixed set per clip.** Pick the harmonics once for the clip. Reselecting the largest terms on every in-between frame makes terms switch on and off and the outline twitch.
- **One normalisation for the whole family.** Scale and centre all shapes of a clip the same way, or the morph also resizes.
- **Mid-way self-crossing.** Two valid outlines can mix into one that crosses itself. Check frames at alpha 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75.
- **Cost.** The plain DFT is quadratic. Fine at authoring time for up to a few hundred samples; do not run it per frame.
- **Corners.** A low budget rounds them. That is a look, not a bug, but say so in the [style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract).

**Sources:** the owner's project and its package notes (private repository); the maths is the standard Fourier description of a closed curve. The demo above runs a real DFT on two polygons. We built the demo and did not run a video through this pipeline.

title: Technique: letters as compound harmonic contours
label: Harmonic type
summary: A glyph is a few closed contours. Fill them as one compound path with the even-odd rule so holes stay open, and draw text from the same primitives as the art.
markdown:
# Technique: letters as compound harmonic contours

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

In the owner's game project the letters are not a font file. Each glyph is a short list of closed contours, stored as harmonics like every other shape ([harmonic morph](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/harmonic-morph)), plus an advance width and an entry and exit point. Text is laid out from those glyphs. The picture and the type then come from one source, with one look.

[Figure, animated on the site: The letters O and A, each with an outer and an inner contour rebuilt from 16 harmonics. Non-zero fill (left) fills the holes in; even-odd fill of one compound path (right) keeps them open.]

## How it works

An "O" is two contours: the outside and the hole. Draw them as two separate shapes and the hole is covered. Draw them as one path with several sub-paths and the fill rule decides. With the non-zero rule, two contours that run the same way both count as "inside", so the hole fills. With the even-odd rule, a point is inside when a ray from it crosses an odd number of edges, so the hole stays open whichever way the contours run ([MDN: fill-rule](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG/Reference/Attribute/fill-rule)).

The project draws a glyph as one compound path with even-odd fill, and sizes text through the font's units per em. Spaces use a stored space advance. A missing character is an error, not a silent gap.

## How to build it

```js
function glyphPath(glyph, scale, x, y) {
  let d = "";
  for (const c of glyph.contours) d += pathOf(contour(c.harmonics, 96), x, y, scale); // M..L..Z each
  return d;                                    // one string, several sub-paths
}
ctx.fill(new Path2D(glyphPath(g, size, penX, baseline)), "evenodd");
penX += g.advance * size;
```

A letter animates like any other [harmonic shape](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/harmonic-morph): its contours can be mixed with another letter's, as long as both have the same number of contours in the same order. Each contour can also go through the [kinetic type](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/kinetic-type) timing.

## Watch for

- **Hole contours too.** Every hole is its own contour in the glyph. Forget it and the "A" is a solid triangle.
- **Missing characters.** Decide the character set before the first draw; fall back loudly.
- **Baseline and Y direction.** The caller owns the baseline and the axis direction. Pick one and test a letter with a descender.
- **Legibility is a visual check.** A low harmonic budget rounds the corners and can make "A" and "R" look alike. The project says recognisable silhouettes are acceptance checks for the consuming game, not something numbers can prove.
- **Licensing.** Letter shapes you draw yourself are yours; do not trace a font you are not allowed to copy.

**Sources:** the owner's project (private repository) and its package notes. Our demo builds two letters from polygons through a real DFT. We have not set a full alphabet.

title: Technique: hatching instead of a flat fill
label: Hatching
summary: Shade with strokes, not with a solid colour. A circle-and-chord recipe, a second crossing pass and the reasons it keeps a drawing from looking digital.
markdown:
# Technique: hatching instead of a flat fill

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A flat fill is the clearest sign of a computer-made drawing. A pencil shades by laying down many short parallel strokes, and the viewer reads their spacing as light and dark. ProdAdvice shows this as a diagram that contrasts a flat fill with hatched shading ([09:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=540s)).

[Figure, animated on the site: The same ball twice. Left, a flat fill. Right, diagonal strokes only on the side away from the light, then a second pass crossing the darkest part.]

## How it works

1. Decide where the light comes from. In the demo it is the upper left, so the shadow is on the lower right.
2. Lay parallel strokes at one angle (45 degrees here), spaced 6 px apart, only where the surface is in shadow. Each stroke runs from one edge of the shape to the other.
3. Add a second pass at the crossing angle over the deepest part only. Two directions read as a darker tone than one.
4. Wobble each stroke slightly with a seeded offset (1.6 px in the demo), so the lines are not machine-straight. Draw the strokes on in order, not all at once, if the shape appears by being drawn.

## How to build it

For a circle the strokes are chords. Lines `x + y = k` cut a circle of radius `r` at distance `d = |cx + cy - k| / sqrt(2)` from its centre, with half-length `sqrt(r * r - d * d)`, so no clipping mask is needed. For other shapes, clip a set of long diagonal lines to the shape and keep those on the shadow side.

Spacing is the tone control. Closer strokes are darker, so a gradient of shade is a gradient of spacing, not of opacity.

## Watch for

- **Hatching that changes direction between frames.** Fix the angle per object and seed the offsets; see [Drawing cadence and a stable seed](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed). Put this failure in your [error log](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/error-log).
- **Shading under text.** Keep the area behind a label free of strokes, or the label loses contrast.
- **Too many strokes.** A busy shape competes with the message. Reserve the dense hatch for one object.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 08:05-09:09. The chord arithmetic and the spacing values are from our demo.

title: Technique: an importance budget
label: Importance budget
summary: Rate every beat 1, 2 or 3 and give level 3 to at most a quarter of them, so the biggest moves still mean something.
markdown:
# Technique: an importance budget

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Animating every line as if it were the point is the most common tell of generated motion: nothing arrives because everything does. The Motionmaxxing director guide fixes it with a budget.

[Figure, animated on the site: Eight beats rated 1, 2 or 3, drawn as bars. Two of the eight (25 percent) are level 3 and carry the scale, the camera move and the sound.]

## The rule

Give every beat, and every line inside it, an importance of 1, 2 or 3. At most 25 percent of the beats may be 3. Level 3 gets the scale, the camera move, the sound and the hardest work. Level 1 is small and quick. When two elements fight for attention, delete one before restyling either. On a line with a number, the number is the hero, at least twice the scale of the line.

## How to apply it

1. Add an importance column to the storyboard table ([storyboard first](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/storyboard-first)).
2. Count: with eight beats, at most two may be 3. The hero moment is one of them.
3. Spend the effort in that order: [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect) the level 3 beats first.

**Sources:** [Tejashmakwana/motionmaxxing](https://github.com/Tejashmakwana/motionmaxxing), `references/director.md` (section 0 and the checklist, item 12) and `SKILL.md`. Apache 2.0 licence.

title: Technique: a clock per motion, accumulated
label: Independent clocks
summary: Change a speed without moving the past: advance each motion's own phase by speed times dt, and give every motion its own clock.
markdown:
# Technique: a clock per motion, accumulated

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The owner's game project moves planets around stars and spins them. Its notes state the rule: orbit and spin speeds advance independent accumulated clocks, so changing a slider changes only future motion and never recalculates the past at the new speed. The ocean waves keep a third, real-time clock, so stopping a planet's rotation does not freeze the sea. It is a game rule, and it solves a real problem in speed ramps and slow motion.

[Figure, animated on the site: Speed goes from 1x to 3x at 2 s. Left: phase = speed(t) * t, so the phase jumps from 2 to 6 at the change. Right: phase += speed * dt, so the phase only changes slope.]

## How it works

If a motion is written as `angle = speed * t`, changing `speed` at 2 s re-scales everything before it: at the moment of the change the angle jumps from `1 * 2` to `3 * 2`. The picture pops. The fix is to store the phase itself and advance it: `phase += speed * dt`. A change of speed now bends the curve and leaves its past alone. Each motion has its own phase (orbit, spin, waves, a camera drift), so you can slow one without touching the others.

For video the phase must still be a function of time, or [seeking](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame) breaks. Phase is the integral of speed, so build a table once and read it:

```js
const fps = 30, phase = new Float64Array(frames + 1);
for (let f = 1; f <= frames; f++) phase[f] = phase[f - 1] + speed((f - 0.5) / fps) / fps;
// renderAt(t) reads phase[Math.floor(t * fps)], or interpolates between two entries
```

Keep one table per motion. A speed ramp is then a few keys in `speed(t)` (eased with [springs](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs) or a [Hermite curve](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/camera-curves)), never a step.

## Watch for

- **Step changes of speed.** A step in speed is a step in velocity: a visible kick. Ramp it over a few frames.
- **Loops.** A [seamless loop](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seamless-loop) needs the phase to come back to a multiple of one turn at the end; check the table's last entry.
- **Sound.** If the sound follows the motion, drive it from the same phase table.
- **Slow motion.** A slow-down is a lower `speed` for a while. Do not render at a lower frame rate and stretch it; use [subframe blur](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/subframe-blur) if the motion needs it.

**Sources:** the owner's project notes on celestial motion (private repository). The table code is our proposal; we have not rendered a clip with it.

title: Technique: kinetic type per glyph
label: Kinetic type per glyph
summary: Treat every letter as its own element with its own spring and a fixed stagger, so words arrive as a rhythm and not as a block.
markdown:
# Technique: kinetic type per glyph

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

One prompt in our database spells out how a poster-style word should arrive: "per-glyph spring (y, opacity, blur). Stagger = 1/16 note at 120 BPM (125 ms)" ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)). The same prompt asks for a slam from below with spring overshoot for the opening line, and for letters that scramble (a seeded shuffle per glyph) and then snap into place on the beat. Another asks for the wordmark to rise letter by letter from a mask line ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Each letter of STEAL is its own element and rises 125 ms after the one before. The ticks under the word are the start offsets: 0, 125, 250, 375 and 500 ms.]

## How it works

A word that fades in as one block has one motion. A word whose letters start 125 ms apart has a rhythm, and the rhythm locks to the [beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid): at 120 BPM, 125 ms is a sixteenth note, so the last letter still lands within the beat. Each glyph carries three animated values (vertical offset, opacity, blur), each from its own [spring](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs) started at `start + index * 0.125`.

## How to build it

```js
const STAGGER = 0.125;                              // 1/16 note at 120 BPM
for (const [i, g] of glyphs.entries()) {
  const k = spring(t - (start + i * STAGGER), 0.72, 0.35);
  drawGlyph(g, { y: (1 - k) * 40, alpha: k, blur: (1 - k) * 12 });
}
```

For the scramble variant, shuffle with a [seeded](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed) shuffle per glyph, never `Math.random`.

## Watch for

- **Too many words.** The same prompt limits the display type to one to four words.
- **Stagger longer than the beat.** Forty letters at 125 ms take five seconds; stagger by word, not by letter, for long lines.
- **Blur you cannot read.** Keep the final frame crisp; blur is for the first 150 ms.

**Sources:** [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547), [0xnicc0-516612](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612) in our prompt database; the snippet is ours.

title: Technique: painted layers, with light and text in code
label: Layered assets
summary: Generate the detailed pictures as separate transparent layers, then let code do depth, light, particles and text. Parallax is the proof it works.
markdown:
# Technique: painted layers, with light and text in code

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Studio Igor's first platformer, drawn entirely in code, scored 2/10; he stopped after 37 minutes and 12 % of a weekly model allowance. His second attempt generated the pictures as images and let code move them ([6:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=369s)). The split is the technique: images carry painted forms and texture, code carries scale, position, light, motion and interaction ([7:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=468s)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Background, subject and foreground are images; light and text are code. Composed, a slow sideways camera moves the foreground by 18 px, the subject by 9 px and the background by 4 px (demo values) while the code layer stays still.]

## How it works

- **Separate by depth.** Generate the background, the subject and the foreground as their own layers, each on a transparent ground with room around the subject.
- **Keep mutable effects out of the pictures.** Glow, shadow, particles, text and water are deliberately excluded from generated images ([19:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=1152s)). Draw them in code, where one number changes them.
- **Move layers by depth.** When the camera shifts sideways, near layers shift more than far ones. That is parallax, and it is what makes flat pictures read as a space.
- **Hold text still.** Text belongs to the code layer, so it never slides with the picture.

## Check before you animate

- **Holes.** When a layer moves, look for gaps at its edges. Draw layers wider than the frame, as the demo does.
- **A clean subject.** Neutral light and no baked shadow, so the lighting you add does not fight the lighting in the picture.
- **A recorded source.** Save each asset with its prompt, model and source reference, so a bad layer can be regenerated.

## Limits

The method suits scenes and cutout characters. Studio Igor rejected AI sprite sheets and cutting one generated character into pieces; he generates separate body parts in an agreed pose and assembles them ([19:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=1152s)). It is not a replacement for frame animation, and the allowance percentages are one creator's account, not a transferable cost.

Details and a proposed experiment for a 5 to 10 s shot are in [Layered art tutorial study](). The author's open [ref2game skill](https://github.com/studioigor/ref2game) describes the workflow.

**Source:** Studio Igor, [YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk) at 6:09-8:59 and 19:12-20:55. The pixel shifts in the demo are illustrative.

title: Technique: line boil, a contour that is redrawn while the shape stays still
label: Line boil
summary: Redraw each outline a dozen times a second with a little wobble, so a still pose looks hand-drawn. How it works, a small code recipe and where it goes wrong.
markdown:
# Technique: line boil

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Hand-drawn animation never repeats a line exactly. Even a character holding still has an outline that trembles, because the artist redraws it for every drawing. Line boil copies that on purpose: the silhouette stays where it is, and only the stroke is redrawn, about 12 times a second.

[Figure, animated on the site: One circle, six drawings. On the left they play in turn, one every 83 ms, which is 12 drawings a second; on the right the same six are laid over each other. The shape does not move, only its edge does.]

## How it works

Two things move on different clocks. The object (its position, size, rotation) follows the scene timeline smoothly. The outline of that object is a separate set of points, and those points are displaced by a small random amount, a new amount for each drawing. ProdAdvice describes exactly this for "otherwise still contours" at 12 fps ([08:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=485s)), and Studio Igor's whale cartoon uses the same effect with "vibrating contours" at about 12 drawings a second ([0:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=49s)).

The displacement is small. In the demo above it is 2.6 px on a circle of 62 px radius, which is about 4 % of the radius. A larger amount reads as shaking, not as pencil.

## How to build it

Our own recipe, not recovered source code:

```js
// one drawing = the same points, each moved by a seeded random offset
function boil(points, drawing, amp, sceneSeed) {
  const rand = mulberry32(sceneSeed + drawing);
  return points.map(([x, y]) => [x + (rand() - 0.5) * 2 * amp, y + (rand() - 0.5) * 2 * amp]);
}
const drawing = Math.floor(time * 12);   // the drawing cadence
draw(boil(outline, drawing, 2.6, 7));
```

Keep the position of the object outside this function. Pass the amplitude as one token of the style (see [Style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract)), so one number changes the whole film.

## Watch for

- **Noise everywhere.** Move only the strokes, never the labels or numbers. A label that wobbles is hard to read.
- **Too large an amplitude.** If the shape seems to swim, halve the amount.
- **A drawing rhythm tied to the file.** The drawing index must come from time, not from the frame number. See [Drawing cadence and a stable seed](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed).
- **Sparkle.** Judge it at normal playback speed, not frame by frame. A single frame always looks fine.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g), and Studio Igor, [YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk); both are analysed in [HyperFrames tutorial study]() and [Layered art tutorial study](). The amplitude figure is from our demo, not from either video.

# Technique: a locked message and a ban list

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The most precise prompt in our database does two things that cost nothing and remove most of the risk. It **locks the message**: six lines "in this exact order", with the instruction "do not soften, do not add filler slogans", and small supporting words (at most 18 characters, never full sentences). And it **bans** a list: "generic AI clichés (brains, robots, neural nets, sparkles), soft gradients, bouncy cartoon easing, particle explosions, stock futuristic HUD, long paragraphs, narrator essay energy, Canva-deck energy, extra slogans, purple/blue neon, glassmorphism" ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)). Other prompts ban the same family: "crossfades, gradients on UI, particles, glows, bouncy easing, dead beats, anything that feels like a template" ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Left: six lines of text in a fixed order, the only words allowed on screen. Right: a ban list, each item struck through.]

## How it works

A model left alone adds slogans and decoration. A locked message takes the writing away from it, so all its effort goes into timing, type and camera. A ban list does the opposite job: it removes the generic defaults that make a piece look made by a template. Together with strict numbers (a palette of three hex values, three named fonts, tracking values) they leave little room for a generic result.

## How to build it

- Write the lines first and number them; each line gets one beat on the [beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid).
- Put them in the [style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract) with palette and fonts as values.
- Add the ban list as a check in the [error log](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/error-log): after each render, look for anything on the list.
- Keep it short; the prompt's list has about a dozen items, not fifty.

## Watch for

- **A message locked too early.** Lock it after you are sure of the story; changing it later is a rewrite.
- **Bans without a reason.** A list the model does not understand gets worked around. Say what to do instead (for example, "springs, tiny overshoot at most").
- **Copy you did not write.** A locked line you did not write still needs a source and a check; see [auditing a video]().

**Sources:** [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547), [0xnicc0-516612](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612) in our prompt database. We have read the prompts, not run them.

label: Lower third
