# Technique: a lower third that stays inside the safe area

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A lower third is a small, repeatable overlay, so its rules are few and strict.

[Figure, animated on the site: Left, a 16:9 frame with a dashed title-safe line and a strap sliding in at the lower left (the name is a placeholder). Right, the clip: lead 0.2 s, in 0.8 s, hold 5.5 s, out 0.5 s, tail 0.2 s.]

## The rules

- **Inside title-safe.** Every pixel at least 5 percent in from each edge (the skill's template uses 6 percent). The lower third lives in the bottom third; the middle of the frame stays empty for the speaker.
- **Still while read.** The motion is in the build-in and build-out. The hold does not move, or moves so little it does not pull the eye (one slow sheen at most).
- **Defaults when none are given:** 1920 by 1080 at 30 fps, about 8 seconds (under a second in, a still hold of 5 to 6 seconds, half a second out), lower left, silent.

The demo's timeline adds a 0.2 s lead and tail as an empty first and last frame; the skill's check looks for empty first and last frames. Its numbers 0.8 in and 5.5 hold fit the quoted ranges.

## Checks

The skill renders over a checkerboard and over dark and light footage, then checks that every word reads on both and nothing shows outside the revealed part of its panel. Do the same with [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect). For a transparent delivery use WebM or `.mov` with alpha; H.264 has none.

**Sources:** [iart-ai/lower-thirds-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/lower-thirds-skills), `skills/lower-thirds/SKILL.md`. MIT licence.

title: Technique: a reveal through the letters
label: Mask reveal
summary: Replace one line of text with the next by turning the outgoing word into a window, so the cut is made by the type itself.
markdown:
# Technique: a reveal through the letters

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

One prompt describes a transition that needs no cross-fade: "BAD PROMPTING IS" replaces the previous line "via mask wipe through the letterforms (the outgoing line is the mask)", with a magenta and green channel split on the cut. The required technique is stated plainly: "destination text revealed by animating a path mask derived from the outgoing word's outlines" ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Left: the outgoing plate with the word BAD. Middle: the word becomes a window and the next scene shows through the letterforms. Right: the window grows until the next scene fills the frame.]

## How it works

The old word is on a plate. To leave, the plate gets a hole in the shape of the word. Through the hole you see the next scene. Then the hole grows (the letters scale up) until the plate is gone. The viewer sees one object, the word, doing the cutting, so the change reads as designed, not as a fade. The mask path is derived from the same outlines that drew the word, so the two cannot drift apart.

## How to build it

In SVG or Canvas, draw the destination, then the plate with the outgoing text as a cut-out:

```html
<mask id="m"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fff"/>
  <text id="word" fill="#000" font-size="54">BAD</text></mask>
<rect class="destination"/>                     <!-- next scene -->
<rect class="plate" mask="url(#m)"/>            <!-- outgoing scene, with the word cut out -->
```

Drive `font-size` (or a scale on the text in the mask) from a [spring](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs) of time, so the reveal stays seekable. Add the [misregistration](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/misregistration) on the cut frame.

## Watch for

- **A thin face.** A light font makes a window too small to see through; use a heavy display font, as the prompt does (Archivo Black).
- **Mask and word out of step.** Use the same size, tracking and position for both.
- **A fade as a fallback.** If the mask is not ready, cut instead; do not fade.

**Source:** [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547) in our prompt database. We have read the prompt, not run it; the demo is our drawing.

title: Technique: print misregistration
label: Print misregistration
summary: Show two offset colour copies of text for a moment on impact frames only, like a badly aligned print.
markdown:
# Technique: print misregistration

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A street-poster look can be made with a cheap trick from print: two ink colours that do not line up. The prompt says when and how much: "on accent frames only, duplicate the text layer offset (±2–4 px) in magenta and acid green at 40% opacity", and "magenta and green may misregister (print offset) by 2 to 4 px on impact frames only" ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)).

[Figure, animated on the site: At the two impact marks a blue and an orange copy of IMPACT appear behind the word, offset 4 px at 45 % opacity, then vanish. Between impacts the text is clean.]

## How it works

The offset copies add a hit to a beat: they make an impact look physical. The rule "impact frames only" matters as much as the effect. If the colour split is always on, it is a style filter; if it appears on the beat and disappears, it is an accent. The values are small on purpose: 2 to 4 px at 40 %.

## How to build it

```js
function drawTitle(t) {
  drawText(ink, 0, 0);                        // the clean text
  const hit = impact(t);                      // 1 on an impact frame, 0 otherwise (from the beat grid)
  if (hit) {
    drawText(accentA, -3, 0, 0.4);            // behind, offset left
    drawText(accentB, +3, +2, 0.4);           // behind, offset right
  }
}
```

Take `impact(t)` from the [beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid) and keep it to a few frames.

## Watch for

- **Always on.** It stops reading as an impact.
- **Large offsets.** Past about 4 px the text becomes hard to read at phone size.
- **Wrong palette.** The prompt pairs two accent colours with one dark background and one white; other hues are banned.

**Source:** [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547) in our prompt database; the snippet is ours.

title: Technique: motion defaults in frames
label: Motion defaults
summary: When nobody says how long a move lasts, use measured medians: opacity 6 frames, entrances 12, blur 7, exits 10 to 13, at 30 fps.
markdown:
# Technique: motion defaults in frames

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A default duration saves a decision on every element. The Motionmaxxing skill keeps a table of medians measured on a corpus of product films, and a rule for when no other information exists.

[Figure, animated on the site: Six defaults at 30 fps. Each bar is one move, with its length in frames and in milliseconds. The highlighted bar (a translate or scale entrance, 12 frames) is the one to reach for first.]

## The defaults

| Move | Frames at 30 fps | Milliseconds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opacity in | 6 | 200 |
| Call to action, supporting move | 6 | 200 |
| Blur in | 7 | 233 |
| Scale out | 10 | 333 |
| Translate or scale in | 12 | 400 |
| Translate out | 13 | 433 |

The skill states the rule as: with no other information, use 12 frames for a translate or scale entrance, 6 for opacity, 7 for blur, 13 to 14 for a translate exit and 10 for a scale exit; treat 6 and 24 frames as the 25th and 75th percentile edges. The median over all moves in its sample is 10 frames (0.33 s). The demo draws 13 for the translate exit, the lower end of the skill's range.

## How to use them

- Keep durations in frames, not seconds, and derive milliseconds when you need them, as in the [timing plan](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/timing-plan).
- Land entrances with an ease-out: the skill reports that most landings cover the bulk of their travel in the first four frames.
- A film built on 20 to 30 frame ease-outs for everything is slower than the whole sample. Start from these numbers, then change one on purpose.

**Sources:** [Tejashmakwana/motionmaxxing](https://github.com/Tejashmakwana/motionmaxxing), `references/motion.md` (rule R1.1 and the duration table) and `README.md`. Apache 2.0 licence. The numbers are the skill's; the demo is our drawing.

title: Technique: a number as a readout, not a slam
label: Number readout
summary: Show a figure small, beside the thing it measures, on the spoken word, with a thin measuring line. It reads as evidence, not as decoration.
markdown:
# Technique: a number as a readout, not a slam

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

In the demo from Andrey Zenin's tutorial, every number is an instrument readout ([2:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg&t=146s)). A thin measuring line and "50 M" stand beside a drop tower. The text is about 3 % of the frame height, not a headline.

[Figure, animated on the site: The same drop tower in two portrait frames. Left, a slam: a large "50 M" over the picture, 8 % of the frame height. Right, a readout: a thin measuring line and a small "50 M" beside the tower, 3.5 % of the frame height.]

## How it works

- **Attach it to the thing measured.** Put the label beside the object and draw the measuring line along it. The number then says what it is without a caption.
- **Make it small.** In our rebuild a readout is 60 to 80 px on a 1920 px frame, which is 3.1 to 4.2 %; the drawing uses 3.5 %. The v3 bond Short set "US$8.8" as a slam of 156 px, which is 8.1 %.
- **Land it on the word.** The readout arrives when the number is spoken, without a slam or a bounce.
- **One per shot, at most.** The demo's other readouts are "TREMOR 0.0", "VOICE" with an even level meter and "100 %" on a popcorn bucket. Each confirms or contradicts the voice.
- **No captions and no headline type** in the excerpt.

## How to build it

```js
const readout = { label: "50 M", size: 0.035 * frameHeight, at: wordStart("fifty") };
```

Make the label and the measuring line one component, so the line and the text always move and fade together.

## Watch for

- **Unreadable on a phone.** Test at arm's length. If it fails, make it slightly larger, not a slam.
- **A count-up on a ratio.** Mid-count it shows a wrong ratio on screen (the bond Short builder saw "1 : 8" on the way to a different value). Show finished ratios.
- **A number the voice already says,** with a label that repeats the voice. Keep a label only where the voice cannot carry the meaning.

This is a proposed change for our shorts, not an approved style rule; it was suggested in [Reference: 2D video plugin]() and has not been audited.

**Source:** Andrey Zenin, [YyUP_hSovOg](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg) at 2:26-2:47; [Skill trial: bond Short]() for the count-up finding.

title: Technique: gradients in OKLCH
label: OKLCH gradients
summary: Blend two colours in OKLCH instead of sRGB numbers and the middle of the gradient keeps its chroma instead of going grey.
markdown:
# Technique: gradients in OKLCH

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Mixing two sRGB colours number by number passes through a dull middle. The colour-motion skill tells you to interpolate in a perceptual space (OKLCH or Lab) to fix "muddy" or grey gradients.

[Figure, animated on the site: The same blue and amber in 40 stripes, mixed two ways. The line under each bar is the chroma of every stripe, computed in the demo from the displayed colour. The sRGB mix dips in the middle; the OKLCH mix does not.]

## What OKLCH is

`oklch(L C H)`: L is perceptual lightness (0 to 1), C is chroma (colourfulness), H is the hue angle in degrees. Keeping L and C fixed while turning H gives hues of about equal visual weight, which is hard in HSL.

## How the demo computes it

The demo converts both endpoints to OKLab with the published matrices, then interpolates lightness, chroma and hue (taking the short way round the hue circle) and converts back to sRGB. The grey dip is measured, not asserted: the chroma line is computed from each displayed stripe. Out-of-gamut values are clipped per channel, which is the simplest choice. In CSS you can ask for the same blend with `linear-gradient(in oklch, ...)`.

**Sources:** [iart-ai/motion-design-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/motion-design-skills), `skills/color-motion/SKILL.md` and `references/palettes-and-interpolation.md` (MIT licence). The colour conversion uses Bjorn Ottosson's published OKLab matrices. The two colours are ours.

title: Technique: one shape, never cut
label: One shape, never cut
summary: Tell a product story with one element that morphs from state to state, driven by a cursor, with no cuts and no cross-fades.
markdown:
# Technique: one shape, never cut

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A group of prompts for product UI motion share a rule: one shape tells the whole story. "Every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur" ([AnnaCher](https://x.com/AnnaCher___/status/2103571098638152174)). "A prompt bar becomes a button, the button becomes a progress ring, the ring becomes a preview window... No cuts, no fades between scenes: objects transform" ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)). "One shape, zero cuts. The shape morphs from state to state and is never replaced" ([flxrnc](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921)).

[Figure, animated on the site: One element in four states, from a mascot to a play button, a loader and a timeline. The dashed ring travels between the cards to show the element is the same one: it morphs and is never replaced.]

## How it works

Because the element persists, the eye follows it across states and the story needs no cut. Size, radius and colour are each a [chain of springs](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs), so a change in one state starts from wherever the last one ended. Content inside the shape is separate: it swaps with a 12 px blur and a fade over 0.15 s ([flxrnc](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921)), and needs its own clip and its own enter and exit timing so text never overlaps ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)). A cursor causes every change with a real click or drag, and its tip stays locked to whatever it drags. The camera zooms so each state fills about half the frame.

## How to build it

```js
const shape = {
  w: chain(springs, "w"), h: chain(springs, "h"),
  r: chain(springs, "r"), color: chain(springs, "color"),
};
// at time t, read each property; draw one rounded rect; then draw the current content inside its clip
```

List the states and their beats first, as in the [storyboard](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/storyboard-first).

## Watch for

- **Cross-fading one colour into another.** The prompt says: do not cross-fade orange into ink. Animate the colour value.
- **Content popping while the shape moves.** Give text its own timing, after the morph has started.
- **A cursor that arrives late.** Aim it at where the target will be when it lands, and keep its speed under 65 px per frame.

**Sources:** [annacher-152174](https://x.com/AnnaCher___/status/2103571098638152174), [0xnicc0-516612](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612), [flxrnc-251921](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921) in our prompt database. We have not run these prompts; the demo is a stand-in drawing, not their output.

title: Technique: parallax from three layer speeds
label: Parallax layers
summary: Move the background at 0.2x, the midground at 0.6x and the foreground at 1.2x, so depth is read from the speed difference.
markdown:
# Technique: parallax from three layer speeds

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Depth in a flat scene comes from layers that move by different amounts for the same camera move.

[Figure, animated on the site: One camera pan of 100 units. The background layer follows at 0.2x, the midground at 0.6x and the foreground at 1.2x. A clipped frame hides what slides outside it.]

## The numbers

The shot-composition skill gives the CSS speeds `--speed: 0.2` for the background, `0.6` for the middle and `1.2` for the foreground. The demo uses them as multipliers of one pan. Each layer is a transform on a group, ending at the resting position.

## Notes

- Give each layer a role: a low-contrast, soft background (ambient), a midground that supports the subject, a sharp foreground (primary). This is our reading, not a quoted rule.
- Use the camera ease the skill recommends, ease-in-out, never linear except for continuous loops. The camera pairs well with the [camera curves](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/camera-curves).
- Parallax is a vestibular trigger. Remove it under reduced motion: see [reduced motion in tiers](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/reduced-motion-tiers).

**Sources:** [iart-ai/motion-design-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/motion-design-skills), `skills/shot-composition/references/camera-and-grids.md` (section "Parallax layering"). MIT licence.

title: Technique: reveal a diagram in order
label: Progressive diagram
summary: Nodes first, then edges, then labels; then keep the active node at full strength and dim the rest to 35 percent.
markdown:
# Technique: reveal a diagram in order

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Showing a whole diagram at once makes the viewer read all of it. Showing it in order makes them read one idea per beat.

[Figure, animated on the site: Three nodes appear, then the two edges with a dot travelling along them, then the labels. Last, node 2 stays at full strength and the others dim to 35 percent.]

## The rules from the skill

- Reveal in this order: nodes, then edges, then labels. Nothing dumps in all at once.
- Highlight the active element and dim the rest (focus and context). The skill's table gives the dim level as opacity 0.35 over 0.3 s.
- Pace to comprehension: hold each step 0.5 to 1.5 seconds so it lands.
- Keep one visual grammar: a colour means one thing and never changes mid-piece.

In the demo the final state is also the resting picture, and each element's entrance and its dimming are merged into one animation. Two animations on one property would let the later one's backward fill override the earlier. See [seekable frame](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame).

**Sources:** [iart-ai/explainer-video-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/explainer-video-skills), `skills/diagram-animation/SKILL.md`. MIT licence. The node names are placeholders.

title: Technique: reduced motion in three tiers
label: Reduced motion tiers
summary: When a viewer asks for less motion, remove the vestibular triggers, shorten the rest to a fade, and keep colour changes and progress.
markdown:
# Technique: reduced motion in three tiers

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is a signal that some movement causes nausea, dizziness or migraines. The accessible-animation skill treats it as graceful degradation, not a kill switch: an instant change with no transition can disorient more, because elements teleport.

[Figure, animated on the site: Three rows, each with the normal version and the reduced version. Tier 1 is removed: the big slide is static. Tier 2 is softened: a slide becomes a 150 ms fade. Tier 3 is kept: a colour fade stays.]

## The three tiers

1. **Remove entirely (vestibular triggers).** Parallax, large slides across the viewport, scale or zoom of large elements, 3D spin, auto-playing carousels and marquees, scroll hijacking, motion paths.
2. **Soften or shorten.** Replace movement with a short opacity fade (200 ms or less), reduce distance and duration. Keep the fact of a transition. The skill's example: a 600 ms slide from the left becomes a 150 ms cross-fade.
3. **Always keep.** Opacity fades, colour changes, focus rings, loading indicators, and motion essential to meaning.

## A sketch

Write the motion as the default and override it under the media query.

```css
.card { transition: transform 600ms ease, opacity 600ms ease, background-color 200ms ease; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .card { transition: opacity 150ms ease, background-color 200ms ease; transform: none; }
}
```

For a video file there is no media query, so keep a second cut without the tier 1 moves if viewers need one.

**Sources:** [iart-ai/web-animation-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/web-animation-skills), `skills/accessible-animation/SKILL.md`. MIT licence. The WCAG reference (2.3.3) is the skill's, not checked by us.

title: Technique: reference by link
label: Reference by link
summary: Give the assistant a link to a clip you like and ask for your own story in that style, instead of describing the style in words.
markdown:
# Technique: reference by link

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The ИИ МАСТОДОНТ tutorial lists this as the first of its four tips: when you see a strong clip, give the link to the post to the model and say "do it in this style, but with my story or prompt"; the author calls it the simplest way to copy any style, and says it used to be almost impossible ([13:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=790s)). He shows it in the cartoon demo, where he pasted a prompt and a link to an X post, and the model went and found the media itself, which older models needed a file path for ([03:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=225s)). For the promo he gave references, then sent the model to look for the best videos made with the same model, "for inspiration", and it came back with a better result ([07:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=443s)). Several prompts in our database do the same: "Analyze [a link] and build a product promo from our own UI" ([AnnaCher](https://x.com/AnnaCher___/status/2103571098638152174)).

[Figure, animated on the site: A link goes in; a short read-out of the style comes out (palette, type, camera, beat grid, cursor, springs); then it is applied to a new story.]

## How it works

Style is hard to put in words and easy to point at. The model reads the clip or its post and extracts a specification: colours, fonts, camera behaviour, timing grid, how the cursor moves. Your content (words, facts, product) is separate. That is the whole contract: **their grammar of motion, your story.**

## How to build it

Ask in two steps so you can check the read-out:

1. "Read this post and write the style as a spec: palette in hex, fonts, camera moves, tempo, cursor rules, what is banned."
2. "Now make my 12 s piece about X with that spec." Keep the spec in the [style contract](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/style-contract) so every scene uses it.

## Watch for

- **Copying the content.** The link supplies style only. Check that no copyrighted frames, words or music came along; see the [style gate]().
- **A read-out you did not see.** Without step 1 you cannot tell whether the model understood the reference.
- **Taking a demo for a guarantee.** The author says a good monteur still does better; treat the result as a draft ([11:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=674s)).

**Sources:** ИИ МАСТОДОНТ, [yEpN_s9UkAE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE) at 03:45, 07:23 and 13:10 (transcript read by us; we have not run the prompts), and [annacher-152174](https://x.com/AnnaCher___/status/2103571098638152174) in our prompt database.

title: Technique: render, then inspect real frames
label: Render and inspect
summary: A quality gate that cannot be argued with: pull frames at fixed times from an actual render, write down what is wrong with each, fix the source.
markdown:
# Technique: render, then inspect real frames

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The creator credits his model with analysing reference clips and checking its own work ([05:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=300s)), and his checklist includes an agent review of frames ([10:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=614s)). Studio Igor adds numbers: scripts measure foot slide, asymmetry, bone stretch and transition jolts, and image critics look at rendered frames ([20:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=1255s)). The shared idea is that an assistant's statement that "it looks right" is not evidence; a frame is.

[Figure, animated on the site: Frames at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 s are checked in turn. The 2.0 s frame has its label at the edge; the defect is logged with its time, the source is fixed and the clip is rendered again.]

## How it works

1. **Render a preview** of the scene, not a mock-up. A saved file is the proof that the check ran.
2. **Pull frames at fixed times:** the opening, a midpoint, a transition and the last frame. For a 5 s clip that is 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 s.
3. **Write one observation per frame, with the time.** "Label touches the right edge at 2.0 s" is a finding. "Looks fine" is not.
4. **Fix the source, not the frame,** then render again and compare.
5. **Watch the clip once at normal speed.** Frames cannot show sparkle, flicker, a missed beat or a bad hold.

A person still decides about meaning, facts and style fit. The loop removes the defects an assistant can see and hands over a short list of what remains.

## Add numbers where you can

Measure what is measurable: contour displacement per frame, text bounding boxes against the safe area, the share of near-black frames. Our [skill trial]() turned scans like these into gates, and every build failed at least one gate in a draft and was fixed before the render.

## Watch for

- **A claim without a file.** Require the preview path and the frame times in the report.
- **Checking only the start.** Defects cluster at transitions and at the end.
- **Fixing in post.** A patched frame hides a source that will break again; correct the scene.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 05:00-06:16 and 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, [YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk) at 20:55-22:50. Both describe the checks; neither publishes pass rates.

title: Technique: a seamless loop
label: Seamless loop
summary: Make the last frame equal the first, including the cursor, so a piece can repeat with no visible seam.
markdown:
# Technique: a seamless loop

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Looping pieces need more than a long fade at the end. Three prompts in our database require "the last frame must be the first frame" ([flxrnc](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921), [AnnaCher](https://x.com/AnnaCher___/status/2103571098638152174), [0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)), and one adds that position, opacity and cursor must match too ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)). The same prompt that asks for a 14 s loop lists the usual failure as a fix: "the cursor jump at the loop wrap" is removed with `t - 14*floor(t/14)`.

[Figure, animated on the site: Two 14 s loops drawn as rings. Left: the last frame is not the first, and the dot jumps at the seam. Right: time is wrapped and the last frame equals the first, so the dot closes the ring.]

## How it works

A loop has a seam where the end meets the start. Anything that is not identical at the two ends shows as a jump: a cursor that ends mid-screen, an opacity that has not returned to its starting value, a spring that has not settled. The fix has two halves. Design the story so it returns to its first state (in the prompts, "the toast turns back into an empty prompt bar", "the toast shrinks back into the mascot"). And make every time-dependent value read the wrapped time, so a frame at `t = 14` is the frame at `t = 0`.

## How to build it

```js
const LOOP = 14;
const wrap = (t) => t - LOOP * Math.floor(t / LOOP);   // 0 <= wrap(t) < 14
window.renderAt = (t) => draw(ctx, layout(plan, wrap(t)));
```

Then compare frame 0 with the last frame, pixel by pixel, as one of the [render-and-inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect) checks. Let all springs finish before the end so the last frame is at rest.

## Watch for

- **A cursor that ends elsewhere.** Park it where it starts, as part of the last beat.
- **A long cross-fade.** It hides the jump but also the story; one prompt bans "crossfades" outright ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)).
- **Springs still moving.** A [spring](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs) that settles at 0.35 s needs 0.35 s of quiet before the wrap.

**Sources:** [flxrnc-251921](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921), [annacher-152174](https://x.com/AnnaCher___/status/2103571098638152174), [0xnicc0-516612](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612), [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547) in our prompt database. The wrap expression is the prompt's; the pixel comparison is our proposal.

label: Seekable frame

markdown:
# Technique: a seekable frame function

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Several of the strongest prompts in our prompt database make the same demand first: the picture at time `t` may depend on `t` and nothing else. One prompt states it as a build rule: `window.renderAt(t)` must be a pure function of time, with no `Math.random`, no clock and no carried state, and `?t=` in the address must freeze the exact moment ([flxrnc](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921)). Another asks for `seek(t)` with no CSS transitions, no `setInterval` and no React state across frames ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)). A third says the same in one line: every frame is a function ([BuildFastWithAI](https://x.com/BuildFastWithAI/status/2108403445304844291)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Top row: five frames computed from time alone, so a jump to 3.6 s gives the right picture. Bottom row: each frame is built from the last one, so after the same jump the ball is still where it was at 2.4 s.]

## How it works

If a frame depends only on `t`, three things become cheap. You can **seek**: open `?t=3.6` and see exactly that moment. You can **check**: render five stills around a beat without playing the clip ([storyboard and pre-pass](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/storyboard-first)). You can **re-render** a single scene and get the same pixels. A stateful animation, where each frame nudges the previous one, gives none of these: a jump lands in a state nobody has computed.

## How to build it

Keep every number that changes in a function of `t`, and draw from it:

```js
window.renderAt = (t) => {
  const p = layout(plan, t);   // positions, opacities, text: from t and the plan only
  draw(ctx, p);                // paint; never read what was painted before
};
const t = Number(new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("t"));
if (!Number.isNaN(t)) renderAt(t);   // ?t=3.6 freezes that moment
```

The export loop then calls `renderAt(frame / fps)` for every frame. Randomness comes from a [stable seed](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed), never from `Math.random`.

## Watch for

- **Hidden state.** A counter, an array that grows, a timer or a transition that keeps running is state. Derive it from `t` instead (a typed text shows `floor(progress * length)` characters).
- **CSS transitions and timers.** They run on the page clock, not on `t`. Do not use them.
- **Changing a target several times.** Do not mutate a value. Add one [spring](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/closed-form-springs) per change.

**Sources:** the prompts [flxrnc-251921](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921), [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547) and [BuildFastWithAI](https://x.com/BuildFastWithAI/status/2108403445304844291) in our prompt database. We have read the prompts, not run them; the code is our proposal.

markdown:
# Technique: one sentence, one shot, cut just before the word

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A code-drawn demo in Andrey Zenin's tutorial shows an editing grammar that carries over to any narrated video ([2:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg&t=122s)). We measured its 28.6 s excerpt with scene detection and word timestamps; the full table is in [Reference: 2D video plugin]().

[Figure, animated on the site: Four sentences and their four shots on a 10 s axis (illustrative times). Each cut lands 0.14 s before its sentence's first word, and the longest pause (0.8 s) comes before the punch line.]

## What the measurement shows

- After the first, 11 of 13 sentences get a new shot. Ten cut at the sentence start and one on the noun the shot shows. The two without a cut play out inside one held shot where the action itself changes the picture.
- The cut comes 0.01 to 0.29 s before the first word, with a median of 0.14 s. The eye sees the new picture a few frames before the ear hears the sentence.
- The pattern is a wide shot, then a close insert of the one detail that carries the sentence. The inserts are short (1.0 to 2.1 s); the wides carry the time (1.6 to 6.0 s).
- Gaps between sentences run from 0.38 to 0.80 s, with a median near 0.48 s. The 0.80 s gap sits right before the punch line.
- The camera does not travel. A closer view is a cut to a new framing, not a push.

## How to build it

Mark sentence starts separately from word times in your cue file. Put shot boundaries on the sentence starts, 0.1 to 0.3 s early. Word cues inside a sentence drive reveals, not cuts.

```js
shots = sentences.map(s => ({ cutAt: s.start - 0.14, hold: s.end }));
```

Give the punch line the largest `gap_before` value. A setup shot shows what everyone expects, a short insert shows what actually happened.

## Watch for

- **Cuts inside a sentence,** unless the sentence is a list.
- **A locked frame with nothing changing.** A static frame is alive only if something inside it changes; our [skill trial]() recommends a change at least every 3 s.
- **Late cuts.** A cut after the word reads as lag. Keep them inside a 0.3 s window.

**Source:** Andrey Zenin, [YyUP_hSovOg](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyUP_hSovOg) at 2:02-2:47. Measurements are ours, accurate to about 0.1 s, from the YouTube file and automatic transcription of a 30 s excerpt the author chose.

title: Technique: a contour spectrum as a voice
label: Shape to sound
summary: Use the magnitudes of a shape's harmonics as the partials of a tone, so the look of a character sets its timbre. All sound is synthesised, so it is deterministic.
markdown:
# Technique: a contour spectrum as a voice

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The owner's game project synthesises every sound from harmonics: no recordings, no sample packs. Its notes describe one link that suits motion work well: the contour of a character is also its voice. A round character sounds nearly like a sine wave; a spiky one sounds buzzy.

[Figure, animated on the site: A circle and a star. Bars: the magnitudes of their first 16 harmonics, normalised. Line: one period of the tone those partials make. The circle is almost one partial; the star spreads over many.]

## How it works

A shape is a set of harmonics ([harmonic morph](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/harmonic-morph)). A tone is also a set of harmonics: partials at multiples of one pitch. The project maps one onto the other. For each shape harmonic `k` it takes the magnitude `sqrt(re^2 + im^2)`, folds the positive and negative frequency together as `|k|`, ignores the centre term, and uses the result as the level of partial `|k|`, at most 32 of them, normalised to unit energy. The browser's `PeriodicWave` builds the waveform from those levels ([MDN: PeriodicWave](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/PeriodicWave)).

Position does not enter, and a uniform change of size only scales all magnitudes, so after normalisation shifting or scaling a character does not change its timbre. Only the silhouette does.

The same notes build short sounds the same way: additive spectra, short amplitude envelopes, pitch sweeps, and percussive texture from three nested sine oscillators instead of random noise. No random number is needed, so the sound is the same on every render.

## How to build it

```js
const real = new Float32Array(33), imag = new Float32Array(33);
for (const { k, re, im } of harmonics)
  if (k !== 0 && Math.abs(k) < 33) imag[Math.abs(k)] += Math.hypot(re, im);
const e = Math.hypot(...imag);
for (let k = 1; k < 33; k++) imag[k] /= e;
osc.setPeriodicWave(audioCtx.createPeriodicWave(real, imag));
```

For a video, render the track offline (`OfflineAudioContext`) so it is exported as a file, not played live. Then a [morph](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/harmonic-morph) can glide the timbre: recompute the levels from the mixed harmonics at each audio block. We have not tried this part; it follows from the mapping.

## Watch for

- **Same shape, same voice.** If a mascot changes shape, say whether its voice should change. A fixed identity wants a fixed spectrum.
- **Level.** Check loudness numerically, as in [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect), and duck under narration.
- **Not a recording.** Synthesised tones are clean. Add an envelope (attack, release) or they click.
- **Live audio in a render.** A live `AudioContext` needs a user gesture and follows the wall clock. Do not use it inside a [seekable frame](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame) pipeline.

**Sources:** the owner's project notes on harmonic audio (private repository). The demo computes the spectra from real DFTs; we did not render audio.

title: Technique: a speed ramp as a time remap
label: Speed ramp
summary: Slow down into an impact and snap back: speed is a curve, the source frame is its running sum, and the slowest frame lands on the beat.
markdown:
# Technique: a speed ramp as a time remap

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A speed ramp is not a cut. It changes how fast the source plays, so the viewer sees slow motion into a hit and a quick release after it.

[Figure, animated on the site: Left, speed against frame: 100 percent to frame 20, an ease down to 25 percent at frame 28, back to 100 percent at frame 40. Right, the source frame, which is the running sum of that speed. The dot moves along it; the dashed line is the impact.]

## The numbers from the skill

At 30 fps: frames 0 to 20 at 100 percent (run-up); 20 to 28 an ease down to 25 percent (anticipation); frame 28 is the impact, on the beat; 28 to 40 an ease back to 100 percent (release). The skill also says to keep motion blur consistent through the ramp, or the slow section looks strobed.

## A sketch

The code below sketches the idea.

```js
// speed(f): 1 → 0.25 → 1. Source frame = running sum of speed.
const s = (a, b, f) => { const t = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, (f - a) / (b - a))); return t * t * (3 - 2 * t); };
const speed = (f) => f < 20 ? 1 : f < 28 ? 1 - 0.75 * s(20, 28, f) : 1 - 0.75 * (1 - s(28, 40, f));
let src = 0; const sourceFrame = (f) => { src = 0; for (let i = 0; i < f; i++) src += speed(i); return src; };
```

This is the same idea as the [independent clocks](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/independent-clocks) article: accumulate the speed, do not multiply it by time. In an editor use time-remap keyframes with smooth interpolation; in a code timeline drive a remap curve.

**Sources:** [iart-ai/motion-design-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/motion-design-skills), `skills/beat-sync-editing/SKILL.md` (section "Retime: speed ramps"). MIT licence.

markdown:
# Technique: a storyboard before code, stills before render

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The prompts and the tutorial agree on order of work. A prompt ends with the instruction: "First show me the storyboard. Then write the code. After the first render, check 5 frames around every beat and fix the issues before the final render" ([flxrnc](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921)). Another: "Render one still per beat first. Fix anything cramped, off-grid or hard to read before the full render" ([0xnicc0](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612)), and "before full render, export one still per major beat (8 frames). Fix cramped type, orphan words, low contrast" ([techhalla](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547)). In the tutorial, HyperFrames shows a set of key frames before it renders, so feedback comes before it spends 10 minutes and tokens on an MP4 ([Mastodon video, 06:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=364s)); the author says the key frames were how he saw it was fine and what to correct ([07:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE&t=433s)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Six beat cards with times, then the flow: the storyboard is approved first, code comes second, one still per beat is checked and fixed, and only then the full render.]

## How it works

A render is the most expensive way to find a mistake. A storyboard costs a few lines and shows whether the story and the beats are right. A still per beat costs a few seconds each and shows layout problems (cramped type, an orphan word, weak contrast) before the long render. Because a frame is a [function of time](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/seekable-frame), stills at the beat times are free to make.

## How to build it

1. Ask for the storyboard as a list of `time, what is on screen, what moves` for every beat on the [beat grid](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/beat-grid). Approve or edit it.
2. Write the code. Keep the beats in the [timing plan](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/timing-plan).
3. Export stills at each beat (and a few frames either side, the prompt says five) and look at them with [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect).
4. Fix what you logged in the [error log](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/error-log), then run the full render.

## Watch for

- **Skipping step 1 because the idea is simple.** A one-line change to the storyboard is cheap; a change to finished code is not.
- **Stills only on the beat.** Problems hide between beats; the prompt asks for five frames around each one.
- **Approving the storyboard in prose.** Ask for times and counts, not adjectives.

**Sources:** [flxrnc-251921](https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921), [0xnicc0-516612](https://x.com/0xnicc0/status/2107217691505516612), [techhalla-498547](https://x.com/techhalla/status/2103411244468498547) in our prompt database, and the ИИ МАСТОДОНТ tutorial [yEpN_s9UkAE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yEpN_s9UkAE).

label: Style contract
summary: Turn style words into numbers (line weight, wobble, palette, cadence) and hand them to every scene, so ten shapes look like one set.
markdown:
# Technique: a style contract

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

"Hand-drawn" is not a style, it is a mood. ProdAdvice's checklist starts with "style DNA" and palettes ([10:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=614s)). Studio Igor shows the same lesson from the other side: a generic request for pixel art fails, and the second try works because it names a 320 x 180 internal canvas, a sixfold scale and palette cycling ([2:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=152s)). Later he has the agent write a "style bible" and send it with every image request ([17:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk&t=1054s)).

[Figure, animated on the site: Four tokens (line 3 px, redraw 2 px, one blue, 12 drawings a second) applied to a circle, a square and a triangle, against the same three shapes with no contract: each picks its own line weight, wobble and colour.]

## How it works

Write the contract as a short list of measurable values and keep it in one file that every scene imports:

- **Paper:** background colour and texture.
- **Palette:** four or fewer core colours.
- **Line:** weight in pixels, and how it varies.
- **Wobble:** redraw amplitude and cadence (see [Line boil](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/line-boil)).
- **Shading:** hatch angle and spacing (see [Hatching](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/hatching)).
- **Type and sound:** the font, and the character of the sound.

Add two or three approved stills as visual anchors, and describe the mechanisms behind them in words, because a prompt that only says "like this picture" gives you a copy of the picture.

## Why numbers

A token can be tested. If the contract says 3 px and a frame shows a 5 px line, that is a defect you can name. "Looks off-style" cannot be fixed by a script or by an assistant that was not in the room.

## Watch for

- **Too many tokens.** A contract of forty values will not be followed. Keep the ones that change the look.
- **A contract copied from someone else's film.** Take the mechanisms (timing, mark types, colour relationships) and make original assets; a reference clip does not give reuse rights.
- **A contract that never changes.** When a review finds a better value, update the file and re-render, not just the one scene.

In this studio a new look still goes through the [style gate]() before client use.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, [YQ01D9xGAnk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQ01D9xGAnk) at 2:32-3:37 and 17:34-19:12. The token values in the demo are ours.

title: Technique: a sharp band that makes a scene look small
label: Tilt-shift band
summary: Blur everything except one horizontal band and a real scene reads as a miniature. Key the band like a camera channel, and seed any grain by frame number.
markdown:
# Technique: a sharp band that makes a scene look small

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Miniature faking is an old photographic trick: shoot from above and blur the top and bottom, and the eye reads the scene as a model, because only small things have so shallow a focus ([Wikipedia: miniature faking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miniature_faking)). Our Tabletop Miniature style uses it as its main look: a single post-processing shader does the tilt-shift band and a depth-based blur together, then tone mapping, a colour grade, a vignette and film grain.

[Figure, animated on the site: A small town from above, blurred except for one sharp band. The band moves down and rests in the middle. Two copies of the scene: a sharp one, and a blurred one that a mask hides inside the band.]

## How it works

The blur size at a pixel (the circle of confusion) is the larger of two values: one from the distance to the band, and one from the scene depth. Inside the band it is zero; outside it grows. The style page uses a 40-tap Vogel-disk gather: for each pixel take 40 samples around it in a spiral, weight each by its own blur size so that sharp objects do not bleed into blurred ones, and sum them.

The band is a number like any other camera value, so it belongs in the same keyed table as the [camera curves](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/camera-curves): move it to the station that matters.

## How to build it

The full-screen shader, as a sketch:

```glsl
float band = smoothstep(uHalf, uHalf + uFall, abs(vUv.y - uCenter));   // 0 in the band, 1 far from it
float coc  = uMaxBlur * max(band, depthCoc);                            // size of the blur disk
for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) {                                          // Vogel disk: golden angle spiral
  float r = sqrt(float(i) + 0.5) / sqrt(40.0), a = float(i) * 2.39996;
  vec2 o = r * coc * vec2(cos(a), sin(a));
  // weight by the sample's own coc, then accumulate colour
}
```

For a flat scene (no depth buffer) the SVG demo above is enough: a blurred copy and a gradient mask.

## Watch for

- **Grain seeded by the wall clock.** The style's first version reseeded its grain on a 24 Hz clock, `floor(uTime * 24.0)`. Rendered at 30 fps, that repeats the same grain on one frame in five, so the picture holds still for a frame and then jumps six times a second. It looked like simultaneous white glints on the water. Seed the grain from a frame counter, `uFrame = round(t * fps)`.
- **Measure, do not guess.** The diagnosis: group the frame-to-frame change of in-focus blocks by frame index modulo 5. One class sat 46 percent below the others, and about 1 percent after the fix. A six hertz peak in the spectrum of that change was 8.8 times the median before and 1.8 after. Do not answer the symptom by lowering the grain.
- **Soft edges of the band.** A hard edge reads as a mask. Give it a gradient.
- **Bokeh and noise from `Math.random`.** The same rule as the grain: derive every random value from the frame number and a [seed](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/cadence-and-seed).
- **Real depth of field is different.** The band is a cheat that works from above. Do not use it on an eye-level shot.

**Sources:** our Tabletop Miniature style page (shader design, the grain pitfall and its measurements); [Wikipedia: miniature faking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miniature_faking). The GLSL is a sketch of our design, not the style's code; the demo is a 2D imitation.

title: Technique: a timing plan as editable data
label: Timing plan
summary: Write when every object enters, moves and leaves as plain numbers on one timeline, so a late correction is one edit, not a new render of everything.
markdown:
# Technique: a timing plan as editable data

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

ProdAdvice's central claim is that a coded animation is editable: the assistant writes the graphics and the motion as code, and you change one value. A graphic on screen at 02:50 labels appearance and disappearance times, movement and colour around a common timeline ([01:32-03:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g&t=92s)). The technique is to write that plan down before any motion exists.

[Figure, animated on the site: A 5 s plan as four bars. A playhead sweeps it, then one number changes (the fact label enters at 2.4 s instead of 2.0 s) and only that bar moves; nothing else is redone.]

## How it works

Give every object one row with its entrance time, exit time, path, scale or rotation, colour change and layer. In the demo:

| Object | Plan |
| --- | --- |
| Coastline | Draws from 0 to 1 s, stays until 4.5 s |
| Location dot | Enters at 1.0 s, stays until 4.5 s |
| Fact label | Enters at 2.0 s (edited to 2.4 s), stays until 4.5 s |
| Clear | Everything leaves from 4.5 s to 5.0 s |

The scene reads these numbers; it does not contain them. A missed interval or a wrong coordinate is then fixed in the plan, and you do not regenerate the clip.

## How to build it

Keep the plan in one object at the top of the scene file, and let every animation take its start and end from it:

```js
const plan = {
  coast: { in: 0, draw: 1.0, out: 4.5 },
  dot:   { in: 1.0, out: 4.5 },
  fact:  { in: 2.4, out: 4.5 },
  clear: { in: 4.5, out: 5.0 },
};
```

Build the timeline so it can be sought: the picture at time `t` depends only on `t` and the plan, never on what played before. HyperFrames works this way with a single paused timeline (see [HyperFrames build rules]()).

## Watch for

- **Numbers hidden inside animations.** If a start time lives in a tween, the plan is not the source of truth. Move it out.
- **Timing that ignores the voice.** When there is narration, derive the plan from measured word times, not from guesses.
- **A plan with no end state.** Always give the last object an exit, or the final frame is whatever was left over.

**Source:** ProdAdvice, [K1Mr5_7Gm3g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1Mr5_7Gm3g) at 01:32-03:05. The 5 s example is the exercise from [HyperFrames tutorial study](); the plan format is our proposal.

# Technique: the vertical safe box

[Motion techniques](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques) · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Short-form apps paint captions, buttons and an action rail over the video. What you place there can be hidden.

[Figure, animated on the site: A 1080 by 1920 frame. Shaded bands: top 120 px, bottom 320 px, right 120 px. Dashed: the centre 900 by 1400 box. The green pill sits inside and is readable; the grey pill sits in the bottom band, under the app interface.]

## The numbers from the skill

For all platforms put the hook text and the key subject in the centre 900 by 1400 box. Reserve the bottom 320 px even if it looks empty in the editor. The skill's checklist: composed inside the 900 by 1400 box, with the bottom 320 px, top 120 px and right 120 px kept clear. A second skill gives looser percentages (top about 12 percent, bottom 20 to 35 percent).

## A thing the numbers hide

A box 1400 high, centred in 1920, spans y from 260 to 1660. The bottom clear band starts at y 1600. So the box dips 60 px into that band, and the real limit for text is y 1600, not the box edge. That is our arithmetic from the skill's numbers, not a line in the skill; check it against the platform you target.

Pair this with [one sentence, one shot](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/sentence-shot) for captions and with [render and inspect](https://production-warehouse.suenot.com/#/techniques/render-and-inspect) to check frames against the bands.

**Sources:** [iart-ai/tiktok-video-skills](https://github.com/iart-ai/tiktok-video-skills), `skills/short-form-video/SKILL.md` (safe-area table and checklist) and `skills/caption-animation/SKILL.md`. MIT licence. Platform interfaces change, so treat the bands as a starting point.
